l: Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_a land [over which His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty shall rule] The Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears is identified as the land over which His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty shall rule.

l: Deity Prince of Saruta, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The Deity Prince of Saruta is an Earthly, male Deity Prince, son of the Heavenly Deities, dwelling at Azaka. At Heaven’s eight-forking road, he offers himself as vanguard to His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty and respectfully serves in that role. While fishing, a hirabu shell-fish catches his hand and he drowns in the brine; this leads to three names: Bottom-Touching-August-Spirit, Gurgling-up-August-Spirit, and Bubble-Bursting-August-Spirit.

l: mirror, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A mirror, revered as the august spirit of the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, is worshipped at the temple of Isuzu and accompanies Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty for his descent.

l: eight-forking road of Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The eight-forking road of Heaven is the place where a Deity's refulgence reaches upward to the Plain of High Heaven and downward to the Central Land of Reed-Plains. The Deity Prince of Saruta stands there to meet the descending august child.

l: Duchesses of Saru, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: bear_name_of Great Deity Prince of Saruta [as the Male Deity the Prince of Saruta] The Duchesses of Saru bear the name of the Male Deity the Prince of Saruta. The women are called Duchesses of Saru.

l: August Descent from Heaven of His Augustness the August Grandchild, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_a unit [of a longer document] The August Descent from Heaven of His Augustness the August Grandchild concerns the command for His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven and rule the Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears. It includes the questioning of the Deity Prince of Saruta and the sending of divine objects and attendants with the august child.

l: peak of Kuzhifuru, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Peak called Takachiho in Tsu-kushi, opposite Kara and sunlit morning and evening, where Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty descended from Heaven.

l: His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness, ancestor of the Kume Lords, attends His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty armed with Heavenly weapons, declares a place exceedingly good, establishes temple-pillars and cross-beams, and dwells there.

l: descent from Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_a descent The descent from Heaven brought His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsu-kushi.

l: dwelling at Takachiho, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Dwelling at Takachiho, on Kuzhifuru’s peak, was established after His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness judged the place exceedingly good and raised it.

l: Azaka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Azaka is where the Deity Prince of Saruta dwells when he goes fishing.

l: the sea, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: contains fish-hook [the lost original hook] The sea is the realm in which His Augustness Fire-Shine has his luck and where Fire-Subside loses the fish-hook. It contains the savoury august road, the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, the fishes, and the crocodiles.

l: fishes, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: serve Deity Prince of Saruta [respectfully] The fishes, both broad of fin and narrow of fin, are gathered and asked to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities. They declare that they will respectfully serve him, except for the bèche-de-mer.

l: bèche-de-mer, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A fish with a slit mouth, bèche-de-mer gives no reply and has its mouth slit by the Heavenly-Alarming-Female.

l: The Curse of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A curse explains that rejecting Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks causes the Heavenly Sovereigns’ august lives not to be long.

l: Divine-Princess-of-Ata, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Daughter of Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor, she meets Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty at Kasasa and is sent to him with her elder sister.

l: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A pregnant princess, also called Divine-Princess-of-Ata, is sent to and weds His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty; nearing delivery, she seals and burns a doorless hall before giving birth.

l: Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_sister_of Divine-Princess-of-Ata [elder sister] She was the elder sister of Divine-Princess-of-Ata and was sent with her to His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty. He sent her back because she was very hideous, although Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor had offered her so that the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity might live eternally immovable like enduring rocks.

l: the Heavenly Sovereigns, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: are_offspring_of the Heavenly Deity [august offspring] Their august lives are said not to be long as a consequence of Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks being sent back and only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees being kept.

l: the august lives of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Sovereigns, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: are not long [down to the present day] They are described as not long. Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor attributes this to the rejection of Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks and the keeping of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees.

l: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees's unborn child, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees's unborn child is presented as either the child of an Earthly Deity or the august child of the Heavenly Deity. Its identity is tested through the circumstances of the delivery in the burning hall.

l: the delivery of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: An imminent delivery occurs in a sealed, burning hall, where Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees gives birth to Three Deities.

l: the hall built for the delivery, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: An eight-fathom, doorless hall is earth-sealed and set on fire by Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees before her delivery.

l: His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine, a prince born when the fire burned most fiercely, is ancestor of the Hayabito, Dukes of Ata. Blessed with sea-luck, he catches broad- and narrow-finned things and owns the original fish-hook. After exchanging luck with his younger brother Fire-Subside, he demands the lost hook back and becomes poorer, guarding and respectfully serving Fire-Subside day and night.

l: His Augustness Fire-Climax, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_a child [born second] His Augustness Fire-Climax is the second child born during the delivery in the burning hall.

l: His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside, also called His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears, is the third-born prince, younger brother of His Augustness Fire-Shine, whose luck is on the mountains. During their exchange of luck, he loses Fire-Shine’s fish-hook and journeys to the Ocean-Possessor’s palace. Identified as Heaven's-Sun-Height, he lives in the sea deity's realm for three years, marries Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, retrieves the hook, and receives tide-controlling jewels. He gives back the hook and overcomes Fire-Shine’s attack by drowning, then saving him. Though forbidden to watch Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess give birth, he peeps, sees her crocodile form, flees, and later answers her song with remembrance.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears is another name for His Augustness Fire-Subside. He is the third of the three Deities born in the fire.

l: the three Deities born in the fire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The three Deities born in the fire comprise Fire-Shine, Fire-Climax, and Fire-Subside, who is also called Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears.

l: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, daughter of the Sea-Deity, delights in His Augustness Fire-Subside and marries him. Pregnant, she comes to him and builds a cormorants’-feather parturition-hall, where she gives birth in her native crocodile shape. After Fire-Subside secretly sees her, she leaves and closes the sea-boundary, later sending him a loving song through her younger sister, Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess.

l: the elder-younger brother relationship, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The elder-younger brother relationship between Fire-Shine and Fire-Subside unfolds through requests to exchange luck, a demand for a fish-hook, and instructions for countering actions.

l: the exchange of luck, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine and Fire-Subside exchange sea-luck and mountain-luck; Fire-Subside fails with sea-luck and loses the fish-hook.

l: fish-hook, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine’s fish-hook is lost in the sea by His Augustness Fire-Subside, who makes replacements. Fire-Shine demands the original, found in the tahi’s throat and given to the elder brother by Sea-Deity’s instruction.

l: the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The Ocean-Possessor’s fish-scale palace lies beyond a savoury sea road; Fire-Subside reaches it by boat and stays above its well for three years.

l: the marriage of Fire-Subside and Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Fire-Subside marries Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, given by the Sea-Deity, and lives in the Sea-Deity’s land for three years.

l: the lost fish-hook retrieval, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: recovers fish-hook [from the throat of the tahi] The Sea-Deity summons the fishes and learns that the tahi likely swallowed the fish-hook because it complained of something in its throat. The hook is found in the tahi’s throat, washed, and respectfully presented to His Augustness Fire-Subside.

l: the tide-flowing jewel, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: drowns His Augustness Fire-Shine [when he attacks His Augustness Fire-Subside] The tide-flowing jewel is used to drown the elder brother when he attacks His Augustness Fire-Subside.

l: the tide-ebbing jewel, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: restores_life_to His Augustness Fire-Shine [after the tide-flowing jewel has drowned him] The tide-ebbing jewel is used to save the elder brother after he expresses grief.

l: Submission of His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: submission_of His Augustness Fire-Shine This unit is titled “Submission of His Augustness Fire-Shine.”

l: parturition-hall, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A sea-shore parturition-hall, built by Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess with cormorants’ feathers, is entered for parturition before its thatch is completed.

l: august child of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess and His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: An august child born to Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess and Fire-Subside, named Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely; his mother leaves for the Sea-Plain and entrusts a nursing song.

l: native shape of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess’s native form is an eight-fathom crocodile, assumed during parturition.

l: crocodile, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: The crocodile was the form taken by Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess during parturition. It was eight fathoms long and crawled and writhed about when His Augustness Fire-Subside peeped at her.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Child of Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess and Fire-Subside, he married maternal aunt Jewel-Good-Princess and begot four children.

l: Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Jewel-Good-Princess, younger sister of Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, nursed an august child, carried a song to Fire-Subside, and later married Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely.

l: His Augustness-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: dwells_in palace of Takachiho [for five hundred and eighty years] His Augustness-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears dwelt in the palace of Takachiho for five hundred and eighty years. His august mausoleum was likewise on the west of Mount Takachiho.

l: parturition, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Parturition began before the thatch of the parturition-hall was completed because Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess could not restrain the urgency of her womb. During parturition she entered her native shape, becoming a crocodile.

l: peeping at Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: Peeping at Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess occurred when His Augustness Fire-Subside stealthily looked at her during parturition. Afterward she felt ashamed, closed the sea-boundary, and returned to the Sea-Plain.

l: wedding of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: is_a wedding The wedding of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess took place after Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess returned to the Sea-Plain. They begot four august children.

l: children of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods)
s: A group of four children of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, ending with Young-August-Food-Master’s alternate names.

A chronological imperial record begins with His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, later Emperor Jim-Mu, advancing east from Himuka, defeating resistance, founding rule at Kashibara, and losing his elder brother Itsu-se in battle. Guided by the Great-High-Integrating-Deity, a cross-sword, and an eight-foot crow, he pacifies the Empire; after his death, Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi kills Tagishi-mimi and succeeds as Emperor Sui-Zei. The record then traces successive rulers through marriages, children, palaces, reign lengths, mausoleums, and the noble lineages descending from them: Sui-Zei, an-Nei, I-Toku, Ko-Sho, Koan, Kō-Rei, Kō-Gen, and Kai-Kuwa. It notes the pacification of Kibi by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko, and expands on descendants who become ancestors of regional rulers, grandees, chiefs, and dukes. Emperor Sū-Jin’s reign includes pestilence ended through worship of the Great-Master-of-Things, suppression of King Take-hani-yasu’s rebellion, tribute, and public works. Under Sui-Nin, the deaths of Saho-biko and Saho-bime, Prince Homu-chi-wake’s worship at Idzumo, clan foundations, and Tajima-mori’s return from the Eternal Land precede the Emperor’s death. Emperor Kei-Kō’s reign centers on Yamato-take’s campaigns against Kumaso, Idzumo, Sagamu, and other opponents; Yamato-take dies after encountering the Deity of Mount Ibuki and transforms into a white dotterel. Sei-Mu appoints Take-uchi Prince Minister and establishes countries’ rulers, boundaries, and departmental lords. Under Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō, divine instructions lead to Korea’s submission and later victory over Yamato opposition. Finally, Ō-Jin’s reign records genealogies, foreign contact, succession roles for Oho-yama-mori, Oho-sazaki, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, conflict after his death, and Ama-no-hi-boko’s descendants and eight precious treasures.

A Heavenly Sovereign and august child of the Heavenly Deity, he leaves Himuka, progresses eastward through many places, gains the cross-sword and eight-foot crow’s guidance, defeats resistance, rules from Kashibara near Unebi, fathers children with I-suke-yori-hime, and lives 137 august years.

His Augustness Itsu-se, elder brother of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, joins the eastward progress, is wounded in the hand by Nagasune-biko of Tomi, dies valiantly at the river-mouth of Wo, and is buried at Mount Kama in Ki.

is_a His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko This title refers to His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, whose reign includes the eastward progress, the conquest and pacification of the Empire, and rule from Kashibara near Unebi. His august years are given as one hundred and thirty-seven.

His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, also called His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-mimi, is a son of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and a Heavenly Sovereign. Threatened by His Augustness Tagishi-mimi, he takes a weapon from His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi and kills Tagishi-mimi, then rules the Empire. He dwells at Takawoka, weds Kaha-mata-bime, begets Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi, lives forty-five years, and has a mausoleum on the Mound of Tsukida.

Son of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and ancestor of the Grandees of Oho, he cannot kill His Augustness Tagishi-mimi because he trembles, then yields precedence to His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and serves as priest.

His Augustness Tagishi-mimi, elder half-brother of the younger princes, weds I-suke-yori-hime after the Heavenly Sovereign’s death. He plots to kill his three younger brethren, but His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi kills him in the slaying of Tagishi-mimi.
Nagasune-biko of Tomi, an enemy of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, raises an army at Shirakata, awaits battle, and his forces wound His Augustness Itsu-se in the hand.

Takakurazhi, a person of Kumanu, possesses a cross-sword in his store-house and brings it to the prostrate His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, explaining that a dream caused it to be sent through the roof.

Ukashi the Elder Brother, a resident of Uda, opposes His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko by trying to turn back the eight-foot crow and building a palace pitfall. Forced into his own trap, he dies, is cut in pieces, and is slain in the slaying of Ukashi the Elder Brother.

Ukashi the Younger Brother, a resident of Uda, warns Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko of his elder brother’s plot, helping expose a trap; he then gives a great banquet to the august army and becomes ancestor of Uda’s Water Directors.

is_ancestor_of the Kume Lords He is an ancestor of the Kume Lords and helps force Ukashi the Elder Brother into the pitfall. He later tells the Heavenly Sovereign about I-suke-yori-hime and communicates the Heavenly Sovereign's decree to her.

weds Princess of Tomi He waits on His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko after hearing that the august child of the Heavenly Deity had descended from Heaven. He presents the heavenly symbols, respectfully serves him, and weds the Princess of Tomi.

I-suke-yori-hime, Chief Empress of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, lives at the River Sawi. Chosen from seven maidens on Takasazhi moor, she serves the Heavenly Sovereign, bears three sons, and later warns them in songs of His Augustness Tagishi-mimi’s plot.
Great-High-Integrating-Deity commands His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko not to go farther inland, then sends an eight-foot crow from Heaven to guide him.
are_subdued_by His Augustness Yamato-take [in the East] Yamato-take is commanded to subdue them in the twelve roads of the East and later subdues those of the mountains and rivers.

The august army of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko travels eastward, becomes prostrate after a large bear appears at Kumanu, recovers when a cross-sword is presented, fights Shiki the Elder Brother and Shiki the Younger Brother, and receives Ukashi the Younger Brother’s banquet.
is_a land It is the place from which His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and His Augustness Itsu-se begin their eastward progress.
Tsukushi contains the palace of Kashihi, where Emperor Chiū-Ai dwells, and the Land of Tsukushi, where Empress Jin-Gō returns and gives birth to the august child.
The Land of Kibi was subdued and pacified by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko, with Harima made the mouth of the road.

is_a village It is reached during the progress of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. A large bear appears from its mountain, causing the august army to faint, and Takakurazhi of Kumanu brings the cross-sword there.

contains Ukashi the Elder Brother [with Ukashi the Younger Brother] His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko reaches Uda after following the eight-foot crow and encountering Earthly Deities. Ukashi the Elder Brother and Ukashi the Younger Brother live there, and the place of Ukashi the Elder Brother's death is called Uda-no-Chihara.
is_a place It is associated with Nagasune-biko, who raises an army against His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. The Princess of Tomi is later wedded to His Augustness Nigi-hayabi.
is_a palace [near Unebi] His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko dwells at the palace of Kashibara near Unebi after subduing the savage Deities and extirpating the unsubmissive people.
is_a mountain It is near Kashibara, where His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko rules the Empire. The imperial mausoleum is on the Kashi Spur on its northern side.

l: the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki
s: The Central Land of Reed-Plains is a painfully uproarious land. The Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity and the Great-High-Integrating-Deity send the cross-sword and direct action to pacify it. It is later ruled from the palace of Izakaha at Kasuga and, after pestilence and military disturbances end, is at peace; tribute is first levied on men’s arrow-notches and women’s finger-tips during Emperor Sū-Jin’s reign.

The Empire is a realm whose government His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko seeks to establish quietly by going east. After savage Deities and unsubmissive people are subdued, he rules it from Kashibara. It then unfolds through successive rule by His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi, His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, Emperor I-Toku, His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine, His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito, Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-futo-ni, Emperor Kō-Rei, Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru, Emperor Kō-Gen, Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi, Emperor Sei-Mu, Emperor Ō-Jin, and Emperor Ko-Sho. Under Emperor Ō-Jin, Oho-yama-mori, Oho-sazaki, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko matter to government and succession.

is_a progress [from Himuka toward the east] It begins when His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and His Augustness Itsu-se leave Himuka. It proceeds through several palaces and lands toward Yamato, involving battles, divine guidance, and the establishment of rule.

occurs_at river-mouth of Wo [after being struck by the enemy's hand] His Augustness Itsu-se's death follows his wounding by Nagasune-biko of Tomi. He dies at the river-mouth of Wo after declaring that he has been struck by the wretched villain's hand.

l: the conquest and pacification of the Empire, Kojiki
s: is_completed_by His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko accomplishes it by defeating Nagasune-biko's forces, overcoming the Ukashi brethren and the earth-spiders, and subduing the savage Deities and unsubmissive people.

involves Nagasune-biko of Tomi Nagasune-biko raises an army against the advancing His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. During the fighting, His Augustness Itsu-se is pierced in the hand and later dies.

l: the slaying of Ukashi the Elder Brother, Kojiki
s: is_caused_by the pitfall His Augustness Michi-no-Omi and His Augustness Ohokume compel Ukashi the Elder Brother to enter the palace he built as a trap. He falls into his own pitfall, dies, and is cut in pieces.

is_performed_by His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi kills His Augustness Tagishi-mimi after His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi fails to do so. The killing follows I-suke-yori-hime's warning about Tagishi-mimi's plot.

The cross-sword, also called Deity Thrust-Snap, dwells in the temple of the Deity of Isonokami; sent through Takakurazhi’s roof, it is presented to Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko before Kumanu’s savage Deities are cut down.
Sent from Heaven by Great-High-Integrating-Deity, animal guides His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko along the Yeshinu river’s lower course and onward toward Uda.
The imperial mausoleum is located on Mount Kama in the land of Ki and is also placed on Kashi Spur, atop the northern side of Mount Unebi, as the burial place of two His Augustnesses.

is_ancestress_of the Departmental Lords of Shiki Kaha-mata-bime was ancestress of the Departmental Lords of Shiki. She wedded His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and begot His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi.
is_a Deity [one] Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi was begotten by His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and Kaha-mata-bime.
Emperor an-Nei dwells in Ukiana palace at Kata-shiha, rules the Empire, weds Akuto-hime, fathers three named children, and lives forty-nine august years.
Daughter of Departmental Lord Haye and Kaha-mata-bime’s elder sister, she marries Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi and bears three children.

His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, a Heavenly Sovereign, afterwards ruled the Empire from the palace of Sakahiwo at Karu. He wedded Princess Futo-ma-waka and begot Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine and Tagishi-hiko. His reign lasted forty-five years; his mausoleum was above the Vale of Manago by Mount Unebi.

has_child two Kings (children of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko) [two children] He was one of the three august children of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi and Akuto-hime. He had two Kings as children, including His Augustness Wa-chi-tsumi.
Child of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko, dwelling at Miwi in Ahaji, with daughters Hahe-irone and Hahe-irodo.
Princess Futo-ma-waka, also called Princess Ihi-bi, married Emperor I-Toku, bore two sons, and founded the Departmental Lords of Shiki.

His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine, a Heavenly Sovereign, was begotten by Emperor I-Toku and Princess Futo-ma-waka, later ruled the Empire, dwelt at Waki-no-kami, reigned ninety-three years, and has an August mausoleum.
His Augustness Tagishi-hiko, begotten by Emperor I-Toku and Princess Futo-ma-waka, became ancestor of the Lords of Chinu, Take in Tajima, and Ashiwi.
Princess Yoso-taho, Oki-tsu-yoso’s younger sister, married Emperor Ko-Sho and bore two august children.

Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko is a deity and the elder of two august children. He is chiefly significant as ancestor of numerous Grandees, the Dukes of Ihitaka in Ise and Ichishi, and the Rulers of the Land of Chika-tsu-Afumi.

Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito, a deity and younger brother of Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko, later ruled the Empire from the palace of Akidzushima at Muro in Kadzuraki. He wed Princess Oshika, begot children including Oho-kibi-no-moro-susumi, lived 123 years, and had a mausoleum at Mound of Tamade.
His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine ruled the Empire from the palace of Waki-no-kami in Kadzuraki. His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: marriage of Emperor Ko-Sho and Princess Yoso-taho, Kojiki
s: is_a marriage His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine wedded Her Augustness Princess Yoso-taho, the younger sister of Oki-tsu-yoso, ancestor of the Chiefs of Wohari.

l: birth of the august children, Kojiki
s: The marriage of Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine and Princess Yoso-taho produces Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko and Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito.
has August mausoleum of Emperor Ko-Sho [at Waki-no-kami] Mount Hakata was the location of Emperor Ko-Sho's August mausoleum, at Waki-no-kami.

l: August mausoleum of Emperor Ko-Sho, Kojiki
s: is_on Mount Hakata [at Waki-no-kami] Emperor Ko-Sho's August mausoleum was on Mount Hakata at Waki-no-kami.

is_a emperor Emperor Koan is identified with His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito. He ruled the Empire, lived for one hundred and twenty-three years, and had his mausoleum on the Mound of Tamade.

Emperor Kō-Rei is a Heavenly Sovereign who dwells at the Palace of Ihodo at Kuruda and rules the Empire. He weds Princess Kuhashi, Princess Chiji-haya-ma-waka, Princess Oho-yamato-kuni-are, and Haheirodo; parents several children; lives one hundred and six years; and has a mausoleum at Umasaka at Kotawoka.
Son of Emperor Kō-Rei, a deity and one of five kingly children, who afterwards ruled the Empire.
Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko, ancestor of the Grandees of Kamu-tsu-michi in Kibi, joined Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko at the River Hi to set sacred jars, then subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi.

Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko, ancestor of the Grandees of Shimo-tsu-michi in Kibi and Kasa, joined Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko to set sacred jars at the River Hi in Harima, then subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi.

is_a mouth of the road [for the subjugation and pacification of the Land of Kibi] Harima was made the mouth of the road by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko as they subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi. They set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima.
is_a land His Augustness Oho-biko was sent there to carry out the Heavenly Sovereign's commands. He proceeded there after the suppression of King Take-hani-yasu's rebellion.

is_located_at Road of Koshi [at its mouth] Tsunuga is the site of the temporary palace built for the Heir Apparent at the mouth of the Road of Koshi. It is also the name later given to the strand where the blood of the dolphin-fishes stinks.

l: subjugation and pacification of the Land of Kibi, Kojiki
s: The subjugation and pacification of the Land of Kibi was carried out by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko. They set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima and made Harima the mouth of the road.

Emperor Kō-Gen, a Heavenly Sovereign also called His Augustness Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru, dwelt at Sakaki-bara and ruled the Empire. He wed Utsu-shiko-me, I-gaka-shiko-me, and Princess Haniyasu, fathering five Deities. He lived fifty-seven years and had a mausoleum at Tsurugi Pool.

His Augustness Oho-biko, an august child of Emperor Kō-Gen, was father of Take-numa-kaha-wake, Hiko-inakoshi-wake, and Princess Mimatsu. Sent to Koshi to quiet its unsubmissive people, he first joined Hiko-kuni-buku in suppressing King Take-hani-yasu’s army, then proceeded to Koshi.
rules Empire [afterwards] Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi was one of the august children of Emperor Kō-Gen. He afterwards ruled the Empire.

is_a land A young girl at the Pass of Hera sang of Prince Mima-ki-iri and warned of plotting and killing. King Take-hani-yasu, who dwelt there, raised an army and confronted the Imperial forces at the River Wakara.

Noble Take-uchi, begotten by Hiko-futu-oshi-no-makoto and Princess Yama-shita-kage, became Prince Minister. He had nine children, ancestors of many Grandees, Chiefs, and Dukes. He interceded for His Augustness Oho-sazaki, sought the Deities’ commands on Korea, prepared for its conquest, and later travelled and spoke and sang for the Heir Apparent.

l: august children of this Heavenly Sovereign, Kojiki
s: has_count five [Deities] The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign numbered five Deities. They included Oho-biko, Sukuna-biko-take-wi-goro, Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi, Hiko-futu-oshi-no-makoto, and Take-hani-yasu-biko.

has_count nine [seven males and two females] The children of Noble Take-Uchi numbered nine, seven males and two females. They included the Noble of Hata-no-Yashiro, Noble Kose-no-Wo-Kara, Noble Soga no Ishikaha, Noble Heguri-no-Tsuku, Noble Kino-Tsunu, Princess Mato of Kume, Princess Nu-no-iro, Kadzuraki-no-Nagaye-no-sotsu-biko, and Noble Waku-go, who were ancestors of various Grandees, Chiefs, and Dukes.
is_on mound Emperor Sui-Nin died after reigning for one hundred and fifty-three years. His mausoleum was in the middle of the moor of Mitachi at Sugahara.

Emperor Kai-Kuwa, a Heavenly Sovereign, dwelt at Izakaha in Kasuga and ruled the Empire. He wed four women, fathered five Deities, four Kings and one Queen, and after sixty-three august years was succeeded by Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe. His mausoleum stood atop Izakaha hill.
Hiko-yumusumi, a Deity born to Emperor Kai-Kuwa and Princess of Takanu, has King Oho-tsutsuki-tari-ne and King Sanugi-tari-ne as children; their descendants include five Deity daughters.
is_a august child [of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and I-gaka-shiko-me] Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe was the child of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and Her Augustness I-gaka-shiko-me. He later ruled the Empire.

King Hiko-imasu, a Deity and child of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and Oke-tsu-hime, wed four women and fathered eleven Kings, including Ohō-mata, Wo-mata, Noble Shibumi, Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi, and Ma-wata. Through these marriages and children, his descendants became ancestors of numerous Dukes, Lords, Chiefs, and regional rulers.

King Saho-biko, child of King Hiko-imasu and Saho-no-oho-kurami-tome and elder brother of Princess Saho-bime, conspired with her against Emperor Sui-Nin to rule the Empire. He made an eight times tempered stiletto for the plot, was slain by Emperor Sui-Nin with his sister, and became ancestor of Kusaka and Kahi rulers.

Princess Saho-bime, also Sahaji-hime, became Empress of Emperor Sui-Nin. Younger sister of King Saho-biko, she was drawn into his conspiracy but revealed it, escaped to the rice-castle, and ultimately followed her brother in death.
Prince of Taniha, child of King Hiko-imasu and Okinaga-no-midzu-yori-hime, weds Lady Masu of Kahakami in Taniha and fathers four children: Hibasu, Matonu, Oto-hime, and Mi-kado-wake.

Princess Hibasu, daughter of King Tatsu-michi-no-ushi, became Emperor Sui-Nin’s Great Empress and wife, bore several children, and was buried at Terama near Saki; her death is not explicitly described.

is_a maiden [daughter of King Kamu-ohone] She is one of the maidens whom His Augustness Oho-usu weds instead of summoning to the Heavenly Sovereign. She is identified as the mother of King Oshi-kuro-no-oto-hiko.

King Noble Okinaga, child of King Kami-me-ikadzuchi and Princess Takaki, wed Princess of Takanuka and Princess Inayori, fathering Princess Okinaga-tarashi, Sora-tsu-hime, King Prince Okinaga, and King Oho-tama-saka; he was ancestor of the Dukes of Homuji and Aso.

Empress Jin-Gō, Princess Okinaga-tarashi, is divinely possessed and promised Korea for her unborn child. She crosses to Korea, gains Shiragi and Kudara’s submission, subdues Yamato, gives birth in Tsukushi, is mother to named children, and dies aged one hundred, buried at Tatanami.

King Hiko-imasu's children included King Ohō-mata, King Wo-mata, King Noble Shibumi, King Saho-biko, King Wo-zaho, Saho-bime, King Muro-biko, King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi, King Midzuho-no-ma-wa-ka, King Kamu-oho-ne, Midzuho-no-i-ho-yori-hime, and Mimi-tsu-hime, as well as children from his marriage to Woke-tsu-hime. The text states that his children numbered eleven Kings and records the ancestry and descendants of many of them.
A Heavenly Sovereign who dwelt at the Palace of Midzu-gaki at Shiki, ruled the Empire, wedded three women, and begot twelve august children, including Toyo-ki-iri-biko and Toyo-suki-iri-bime.

His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi was a Heavenly Sovereign, child of His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe and Her Augustness Princess Mimatsu, who ruled Yamato from Tama-kaki palace in Shiki. He married Princess Sahaji, Princess Hibasu, and Empress Princess Saho-bime; faced the conspiracy of King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime; and oversaw Prince Homo-tsu-wake’s upbringing and worship at Idzumo. He had sixteen children, including successor His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, constructed pools, reigned 153 years, and was buried at Sugahara.
is_a Great August Deity Yamato-take enters this deity’s temple and worships the deity’s court before speaking with Yamato-hime.

is_a pestilence [arising during the Heavenly Sovereign's reign] It arose during the reign of His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe, causing the people to die as if none would be left. It ceased altogether after the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things was worshipped and the Earthly Deities were established and honored.

rules Empire [during the reign in which the great pestilence arose] The Heavenly Sovereign grieved over the great pestilence and received the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things in an august dream. He ordered Oho-tata-ne-ko to worship the Great Deity of Great Miwa and commanded other rites, after which the country was tranquil. He also directed military action against King Take-hani-yasu and received reports after the campaigns.

is_a Deity [worshipped at Great Miwa on Mount Mimoro] He appeared to the Heavenly Sovereign in an august dream and said that the pestilence was his august doing. He required worship by Oho-tata-ne-ko, after which the divine spirit did not arise and the land was tranquillized.

Oho-tata-ne-ko, discovered in Minu in Kafuchi, identified himself by genealogy as a child of Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things through Iku-tama-yori-bime. He became high priest of the Great Deity of Great Miwa on Mount Mimoro and was said to ancestrally link the Dukes of Miwa and Kamo.
Iku-tama-yori-bime, daughter of His Augustness Suwe-tsu-mimi and wife of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things, becomes pregnant by a divine youth and bears Oho-tata-ne-ko.

is_a shrine [on Mount Mimoro] It was the place whose Great Deity was worshipped by Oho-tata-ne-ko as high priest. The name Miwa was explained by the three twists of hemp remaining after Iku-tama-yori-bime followed the thread to the deity's shrine.
has Great Miwa [shrine of the deity] It was the mountain on which the Great Deity of Great Miwa was worshipped by Oho-tata-ne-ko.
His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-wake, son of His Augustness Oho-biko, is sent eastward through twelve circuits to quiet unsubmissive people, then meets his father in Ahidzu.

l: twelve circuits to the eastward, Kojiki
s: contain unsubmissive people The Heavenly Sovereign commands Yamato-take to subdue and pacify their savage Deities and unsubmissive people.

King Take-hani-yasu, the Heavenly Sovereign's half-brother and king of Yamashiro, was suspected of plotting a foul act, raised opposing armies, confronted Imperial forces, missed Hiko-kuni-buku with an arrow, and was killed by Hiko-kuni-buku.
Ancestor of the Grandees of Wani, he joined His Augustness Oho-biko against King Take-hani-yasu, killed the king with an arrow, and caused the opposing army to rout.

separates two opposing armies [with the river between them] The River Wakara in Yamashiro separated King Take-hani-yasu's army from the forces of His Augustness Oho-biko and His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku. The two armies confronted and challenged each other across it.

are_separated_by River Wakara [while confronting each other] They confronted each other with the River Wakara between them. After King Take-hani-yasu was killed, his army was routed, pursued, and cut down, while the Imperial forces completed the pacification.

is_prosperous prosperity [after pacification] They died in great numbers during the pestilence, as if none were to be left. After the pestilence ceased and the rebellions were suppressed, they flourished and the Empire was prosperous.

Pacification of the Empire was achieved through worship, rites, and campaigns against King Take-hani-yasu and other unsubmissive people; commanders reported afterward, bringing peace throughout the Empire and prosperity among the people.

l: august mausoleum of Emperor Sū-Jin, Kojiki
s: is_located_at Yamanobe road [on the mound at its corner] It was on the mound at the corner of the Yamanobe road.

Emperor Sū-Jin's reign saw a pestilence ended by religious rites, campaigns that restored peace, the first tribute levied on men's arrow-notches and women's finger-tips, and construction of the Pools of Yosami and Sakawori at Karu.
Emperor Sū-Jin is recorded as having lived one hundred and sixty-eight august years and having an august mausoleum on a mound at the Yamanobe road corner.
Son of Emperor Sui-Nin and Princess Hibasu, His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake later rules the Land of Yamato.
Yamato-hime, Yamato-take’s aunt at Ise, gives him garments for disguise, then equips him with the Herb-Quelling-Sabre and an august bag before his eastern expedition.

Prince Homu-chi-wake, son of Emperor Sui-Nin and Princess Saho-bime, was born during the burning of the rice-castle and named for it. Reared by old and young bathing-women under his mother’s instructions, he initially could not speak, but spoke after worshipping the Great Deity of Idzumo.
Tajima-mori is sent by Emperor Sui-Nin to Eternal Land for the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree. He returns with it after the Emperor’s death, then wails and weeps himself to death.

Yamato is a land called the most secluded and delightful in Yamato-take’s Land-Regretting Songs, associated with a Heavenly Sovereign’s august interment. After the Korean expedition, Empress Jin-Gō returns there, deceives its doubtful people with a mourning-vessel and false report, and defeats the opposing forces.

contains Great August Deity of Ise [temple of the deity] Yamato-take goes into the temple of the Great August Deity of Ise before beginning his eastern expedition and speaks with his aunt Yamato-hime.
contains Princess Miyadzu [house of the princess] Yamato-take visits the house of Princess Miyadzu, ancestress of its rulers, and later returns there after his campaigns.

contains Great Deity of Idzumo [worshipped by Prince Homu-chi-wake] Idzumo was the land where Prince Homu-chi-wake worshipped the Great Deity of Idzumo. It was also where the ancestor of its rulers prepared a temporary palace and food for the prince.
The Eternal Land was the country to which Tajima-mori traveled to obtain the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree.

causes Homu-chi-wake's speech [through a curse relieved by worship] The Great Deity of Idzumo was identified through divination as the source of Prince Homu-chi-wake's affliction. After the prince worshipped this Deity, he gained the ability to speak.

is_built_by King Saho-biko [to await Emperor Sui-Nin's attack] The rice-castle was built by King Saho-biko to await Emperor Sui-Nin's attack. Princess Saho-bime fled there, and Prince Homu-chi-wake was born during the castle's burning.

is_made_by King Saho-biko [for use against Emperor Sui-Nin] The eight times tempered stiletto was made by King Saho-biko and given to Princess Saho-bime so that she could kill Emperor Sui-Nin in his sleep. She lifted it three times but could not cut him.

occurs_in rice-castle [during the conspiracy against Emperor Sui-Nin] Homu-chi-wake's birth occurred while Princess Saho-bime was in the rice-castle during the conflict with Emperor Sui-Nin. His name referred to his birth during the castle's burning and in the midst of fire.

is_led_by King Saho-biko [with Princess Saho-bime] The conspiracy against Emperor Sui-Nin was devised by King Saho-biko, who urged Princess Saho-bime to kill the Emperor and rule the Empire with him. Princess Saho-bime disclosed the plan after she was unable to carry out the killing.

l: death of King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime, Kojiki
s: is_caused_by Emperor Sui-Nin [after the failed conspiracy] King Saho-biko was slain by Emperor Sui-Nin after the conflict at the rice-castle. Princess Saho-bime followed her elder brother in death.

Homu-chi-wake did not speak until he heard the cry of a high-flying swan and later still remained unable to speak. After worshipping the Great Deity of Idzumo, he spoke about the imitation green-leafed mountain in the river.

l: worship of the Great Deity of Idzumo, Kojiki
s: enables Homu-chi-wake's speech [after the worship was completed] Prince Homu-chi-wake was sent to worship the Great Deity of Idzumo with Prince Ake-tatsu and Prince Una-kami attending him. After the worship was completed, he became able to speak.

l: Tajima-mori's return from the Eternal Land, Kojiki
s: Tajima-mori returned from the Eternal Land with eight portions of clubmoss and eight spears bearing the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree. By then Emperor Sui-Nin had died, so Tajima-mori divided the offerings between the Great Empress and the Emperor's mausoleum.
The text does not explicitly describe the death of Princess Hibasu. It states that she was buried in the mausoleum of Terama near Saki when she was the Great Empress.

l: fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree, Kojiki
s: is_called orange [in the present time of the text] The fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree was brought from the Eternal Land by Tajima-mori. The text identifies this fruit as what is now called the orange.

The cry of a high-flying swan prompted Prince Homu-chi-wake's first utterance. Emperor Sui-Nin sent Yamanobe-no-Ohotaka to pursue and catch the swan, which was eventually taken at the Estuary of Wanami.

A Heavenly Sovereign dwelling at Hishiro in Makimuku who rules the Land of the Eight Great Islands. He marries Elder Lady of Inabi and Princess Ka-guro, fathers numerous children including Wo-usu and Yamato-take, lives one hundred and thirty-seven years, and is buried above Yamanobe road.
Empress Kei-Kō is classified as an Empress, but the records only link genealogies and note no separate description.

His Augustness Yamato-take, also called Yamato-wo-guna, is Heir Apparent and an august child of Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake. He subdues the Kumaso and Idzumo bravoes, rulers of Sagamu, and the East’s savage Deities and unsubmissive people, using the Herb-Quelling-Sabre and august bag. He weds Princess Oto-tachibana and has several children by her and other wives. After illness following Mount Ibuki, he dies at Nobe, becomes a white dotterel, and is buried in the August-Mausoleum of the White-Bird.
Heir Apparent and ancestor of Dukes of Mori, he kills his elder brother, then disguises himself to kill the Kumaso bravoes and is praised as Yamato-take.
Princess Ka-guro, daughter of King Princess Sume-iro-oho-naka-tsu-hiko, marries Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake and bears King Oho-ye.
He is the name by which His Augustness Wo-usu is praised after killing the Kumaso bravoes. He later undertakes campaigns in the East, dies after illness, and is transformed into a white dotterel.

is_a bravoes [two unsubmissive and disrespectful men in the West] They are two unsubmissive and disrespectful men in the West. His Augustness Wo-usu disguises himself as a young girl, enters their cave, and kills them.
Princess Miyadzu, ancestress of the Rulers of Wohari, is pledged marriage by Yamato-take, who later leaves his august sword at her house before Mount Ibuki.
Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana, Yamato-take’s Empress, bears his august children, helps build his mausoleum, and pursues him after he becomes a white dotterel.
Yamato-take’s Empress enters Hashiri-midzu sea in his place to still its waves, leaves the Empress’s comb on the beach after death, and later bears King Waka-take.
A deity of Mount Ibuki appears as a white boar, brings heavy ice-rain against Yamato-take after his boast, and leaves him ill.
Deity, son of His Augustness Yamato-take and Princess Futaji-no-iri, later rules the Empire.
is_a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai [two Deities] King Kagosaka is a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai. While seeking an omen at the moor of Toga, he climbs an oak-tree and is devoured when a large boar overturns it.

is_a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai [two Deities] King Oshikuma is a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai and opposes Empress Jin-Gō on her return to Yamato. Pursued after his army is defeated, he and Noble Isahi plunge into the sea and die together.
is_a land [containing a man braver than the Kumaso bravoes] It is described by the Kumaso bravo as having a man braver than themselves, namely Yamato-take.

Land of Kumaso is a land in the West, west of Japan. It is associated with Kumaso, the two bravoes Yamato-take is sent to slay, and later becomes the country Emperor Chiū-Ai prepares to smite before Empress Jin-Gō’s divine possession reveals a promised land farther west.

contains Yakidzu [place named after the burning of the moor] The Ruler of Sagamu deceives Yamato-take by claiming that a violent Deity lives in a lagoon. Yamato-take survives the ruler’s attempt to burn him in a moor and kills the rulers of the land.

is_crossed_by His Augustness Yamato-take [with an august ship] Its Deity raises violent waves that prevent Yamato-take’s ship from crossing. Princess Oto-tachibana enters the sea in his place, after which the waves go down.
contains Deity of Mount Ibuki Yamato-take goes to take its Deity empty-handed. The encounter with the Deity leaves him afflicted by heavy ice-rain and illness.
is_a sabre [bestowed by Her Augustness Yamato-hime] Her Augustness Yamato-hime gives it to Yamato-take before his eastern expedition. He later leaves it in Princess Miyadzu’s house.

contains fire-striker [in an emergency] Her Augustness Yamato-hime gives it to Yamato-take with instructions to open it in an emergency. When trapped by fire in Sagamu, he finds a fire-striker inside.

Yamato-take uses an august sword to cut through burning herbage in Sagamu. He later finds another august sword that he had left at the single pine-tree on Cape Wotsu and sings about the sword placed at the maiden’s bedside.

is_a transformed dead prince [eight fathoms long] After Yamato-take dies, he turns into a white dotterel eight fathoms long and flies toward the shore. The bird is pursued, buried, and then flies away again toward Shiki.
contains Empress's comb [made after the Empress entered the sea] Yamato-take’s Empresses and children build an august mausoleum and perform songs and lamentations during his interment.

contains His Augustness Yamato-take [at Shiki in the land of Kafuchi] The mausoleum made at Shiki in the land of Kafuchi is called the August-Mausoleum of the White-Bird after Yamato-take becomes a white dotterel.
are_subdued_by His Augustness Yamato-take [of the Eastern Lands] Yamato-take is sent to pacify unsubmissive people in the twelve roads of the East and in the eastern lands.

is_a expedition [to subdue the East] The expedition takes Yamato-take through Wohari, the eastern lands, Sagamu, the sea of Hashiri-midzu, Ashigara, Kahi, Shinanu, and back to Wohari. During it he subdues Deities and people, survives attacks, and eventually returns ill.
is_a death [at the moor of Nobe] Yamato-take dies after becoming gravely ill during his return journey. His Empresses and children build an august mausoleum and perform songs at his interment.

l: Yamato-take's transformation into a white bird, Kojiki
s: is_a transformation [after death] After his death, Yamato-take turns into a white dotterel and flies away. His family pursues the bird, builds mausoleums, and records songs associated with the interment.
is_a genealogies The unit records the wives, children, and descendants of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, including the lines leading to several rulers and territorial ancestors.

is_a genealogies Yamato-take has six august children, including His Augustness Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko, King Waka-take, King Ine-yori-wake, King Take-kahiko, King Ashi-kagami-wake, and King Okinaga-ta-wake. The unit traces subsequent descendants through King Kuhi-mata-naga-hiko and later generations.

Emperor Sei-Mu, the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko, ruled from Taka-anaho, wed Lady Oho-takara, fathered King Wata-nuke, elevated Take-uchi, established governance, lived ninety-five years, and was buried near Saki.
Lady Oho-takara, Take-oshiyama-tari-ne’s daughter, weds Emperor Sei-Mu and bears King Wata-nuke.
King Wata-nuke, an august child and Deity, was begotten by Emperor Sei-Mu, Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko, and Lady Oho-takara.

Emperor Chiū-Ai is a Heavenly Sovereign who dwells at Toyora and Kashihi, rules the Empire, weds Oho-naka-tsu-hime and Empress Jin-Gō, fathers four sons, and dies aged fifty-two after refusing a divine promise concerning Korea; he is buried at Nagaye.

Oho-tomo-wake, also called Homuda-wake, is the child of Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō and Heir Apparent. Before birth he is destined to rule countries; his birth bears an elbow-pad-like arm protuberance.

Emperor Ō-Jin, also called Homuda-wake or Heavenly Sovereign Homuda, is the Heir Apparent Oho-tomo-wake whose future rule was foreknown in the womb. He rules the Empire from the palace of Akira at Karushima, marries several queens and princesses, and has twenty-six children. His Augustness Oho-sazaki is identified as his successor, and Ō-Jin grants Princess Kaminaga to him. The account proceeds through Ō-Jin’s genealogies, marriages, descendants, deeds, succession arrangements, intoxication by great august liquor, death, age, and burial.

The Heir Apparent, child of Empress Jin-Gō, is placed in a mourning-vessel en route to Yamato, later travels with Noble Take-uchi, dwells temporarily at Tsunuga, and exchanges names with Great Deity Izasa-wake.

are_carried_by fishes of the sea-plain [great and small] The august vessels cross the great sea after the prescribed offerings and preparations are made. The fishes of the sea-plain carry them on their backs, and a strong favourable wind drives them toward Korea.
Land of Shiragi reaches and submits to Empress Jin-Gō, becomes feeder of the august horses, and is ruled by its chieftain, who promises yearly service and provisions.

Land of Kudara becomes a crossing store after Empress Jin-Gō secures submission during the Korean expedition. It sends tribute: stallion, mare, cross-sword, large mirror, Confucian Analects, and Thousand Character Essay, with Achi-kishi and Wani-kishi as intermediaries.

contains Heir Apparent [during the feigned report of his death] The mourning-vessel carries the august child while Empress Jin-Gō returns toward Yamato. A report is spread that the child is dead, causing King Oshikuma to mistake the vessel for an empty one.
Noble Isahi, ancestor of the Kishi Clan of Naniha and King Oshikuma’s generalissimo, fights Empress Jin-Gō’s forces, is pursued with Oshikuma, and dies with him in the sea.

Naniha-ne-ko-take-furu-kuma, generalissimo for the Heir Apparent, is ancestor of the Grandees of Wani. He feigns submission to deceive King Oshikuma’s forces, restores his army’s bows, then pursues and defeats the opposing army.
Great Deity Izasa-wake dwells at Tsunuga, appears in a dream to exchange names with the Heir Apparent, and is honoured as Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity after dolphin-fishes arrive.
Great august liquor, distilled by Susukori and Empress Jin-Gō, is presented to the Heir Apparent as Empress Jin-Gō and Noble Take-uchi sing and praise it.

l: possession of Korea divinely promised, Kojiki
s: is_a divine promise The possession of Korea divinely promised is announced through the divinely possessed Empress Jin-Gō. The Deities declare that the land is to be ruled by the august child in her womb and prescribe offerings, vessels, and other preparations for crossing the sea.

l: preparations for the conquest of Korea, Kojiki
s: Preparations for the conquest of Korea begin with purification and offerings to Heavenly, Earthly, mountain, river, and sea Deities. August spirits are placed on the vessel; podocarpus macrophylla ashes are put in gourds; chopsticks and leaf platters are made; an army is equipped and marshalled.

is_a conquest [of Korea] Empress Jin-Gō conquers Korea by reaching Shiragi, securing its chieftain's submission, and establishing Shiragi as feeder of the august horses and Kudara as the crossing store. She appoints guardian Deities and crosses back to Tsukushi.

is_a subjugation [of Yamato] Empress Jin-Gō subdues Yamato while concealing the survival of the august child in a mourning-vessel. Her forces defeat King Oshikuma's army at Sasanami, and King Oshikuma and Noble Isahi die in the sea.

l: Heir Apparent exchanges names with the Great Deity Izasa-Wake, Kojiki
s: is_a name exchange The Heir Apparent exchanges names with Great Deity Izasa-wake at Tsunuga after the Deity appears in a dream. The exchange is followed by the presentation of dolphin-fishes as august food and the Heir Apparent's new association with the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity.

l: death of Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō, Kojiki
s: The death of Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō: Chiū-Ai dies aged fifty-two after angering the Deities by rejecting their message, and Jin-Gō later dies aged one hundred; each is buried at a named place.

His Augustness Oho-yama-mori, son of Emperor Ō-Jin, was assigned government of the mountains and sea. After the Emperor’s death, he sought the Empire by attacking Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, but drowned at Kawara Point and was buried on Nara mountain.

His Augustness Oho-sazaki, Emperor Ō-Jin’s son and heir apparent, is assigned to administer the realm. After Ō-Jin’s death, he warns Uji-no-waki-iratsuko of an attack, cedes the Empire to him, and rules it after his death.

Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, Emperor Ō-Jin’s intended successor, was designated to rule Heaven’s sun, defeated Oho-yama-mori after Ō-Jin’s death, repeatedly ceded the Empire with Oho-sazaki, then died early; Oho-sazaki succeeded him.

is_a place Uji is the place whose moor the Heavenly Sovereign gazed upon after crossing into Afumi. Uji also appears in the name Uji-no-waki-iratsuko and in the song referring to the Uji ferry and its river-bank.

l: Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi, Kojiki
s: Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi is the mound where Emperor Ō-Jin’s august mausoleum is located.

The succession was assigned by Emperor Ō-Jin to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, while His Augustness Oho-yama-mori was assigned the mountains and sea and His Augustness Oho-sazaki the government of the realm. After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko repeatedly ceded the Empire to each other until Uji-no-waki-iratsuko died.

l: the eight precious treasures of Ama-no-hi-boko, Kojiki
s: The eight precious treasures of Ama-no-hi-boko are eight articles, pearls, scarves, and mirrors, called the Eight Great Deities of Idzushi.

Ama-no-hi-boko, child of Shiragi’s ruler, crossed from Shiragi to Japan pursuing his wife, landed in Tajima, married Saki-tsu-mi, brought eight precious treasures, and became ancestor of the descendants described.

lasts one hundred and thirty years [according to the emperor's august years] During Emperor Ō-Jin’s reign, the Fisher Tribe, Mountain Tribe, Mountain Warden Tribe, and Ise Tribe were established, the Pool of Tsurugi and Pool of Kudara were made, and people and tribute came from Shiragi and Kudara.

l: the death of Emperor Ō-Jin, Kojiki
s: occurs after the emperor's reign After the death of Emperor Ō-Jin, His Augustness Oho-sazaki followed the Heavenly Sovereign’s commands and ceded the Empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. The death was followed by Oho-yama-mori’s attempted attack and the later mutual ceding of the Empire by Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko.

After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, Oho-yama-mori defied the succession command favoring Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, attacked and drowned; afterward Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko repeatedly ceded the Empire to each other.

ends_at Tajima [after being prevented from entering Naniha] Ama-no-hi-boko’s crossing to Japan followed his wife’s flight from Shiragi to Japan. He pursued her, was prevented by the Deity of the passage from entering Naniha, and then landed in the country of Tajima.
is one hundred and thirty years [august years of Emperor Ō-Jin] The emperor’s age was one hundred and thirty august years.
is_located_at Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi [mound of Mofusu] The emperor’s mausoleum is on the mound of Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: This portion of the Kojiki traces imperial succession from Emperor Nin-Toku through Empress Sui-Ko, combining genealogies, reigns, conflicts, marriages, songs, public acts, deaths, and burials. Nin-Toku rules from Takatsu in Naniha, undertakes public works, remits and later restores taxes and forced labour, and faces domestic conflict involving Empress Iha-no-hime, Princess Kuro, Yata-no-waki-iratsume, Queen Medori, and King Hayabusa-wake. He dies at eighty-three and is buried at Mozu. His successors include Ri-Chiu, saved from a palace fire set by King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu; Han-Zei, noted for extraordinary height; and in-Giyō, who is cured by a Korean physician and reforms surnames and gentile names. In-Giyō’s son King Karu falls after violating Karu-no-oho-iratsume and dies with Queen So-tohoshi. Later dynastic violence includes an-Kō’s killing of King Oho-kusaka, King Ma-yowa’s murder of an-Kō, and Prince Oho-hatsuse’s killings, which force Kings Ohoke and Woke into hiding. Yū-Riyaku’s reign includes marriages, clan foundations, encounters, progresses, and songs. After childless Sei-Nei dies, Ohoke and Woke are found in Harima; Woke defeats Grandee Shibi and receives the Empire after Ohoke yields it. Ken-Zō recovers his father King Ichinobe’s bones and avenges him, followed by Nin-Ken and childless Mu-Retsu. Ohodo becomes Kei-Tai, whose forces kill the rebellious Ihawi. The narrative then gives successions and offspring for Kan-an, Sen-Kuwa, Kim-Mei, Bi-Datsu, Yōmei, and Su-Jun, ending with Empress Sui-Ko’s thirty-seven-year reign and the removal of her mausoleum to Shinaga.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_translated_by Basil Hall Chamberlain It presents an account of Emperor Nin-Toku, his marriages, his children, and the succession of some of his sons to rule the Empire.

l: Emperor Nin-Toku, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Nin-Toku is a Heavenly Sovereign who lived in the palace of Takatsu at Naniha and ruled the Empire. He married Empress Her Augustness Iha-no-hime, Princess Kami-naga, and younger half-sisters Yata-no-waki-iratsume and Uji-no-waki-iratsume; his marriages produced six august children, while those to his half-sisters produced none. He established tribes as proxies for the Empress, heirs, children, and Yata-no-waki-iratsume. His reign included embankments, granaries, pools, channels leading waters to the sea, and a port, using Hada people for labour. He remitted taxes and forced labour for three years, restoring them after prosperity returned, and was praised as Emperor-Sage. Later relationships and conflict led him to follow the Empress into Yamashiro and order an army against King Hayabusa-wake and Queen Medori. He died aged eighty-three and was buried on the Ear-Moor of Mozu.

l: Empress Her Augustness Iha-no-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a_daughter_of Kadzuraki-no-sotsu-biko She was the daughter of Kadzuraki-no-sotsu-biko and was wedded by Emperor Nin-Toku. She bore him four august children.

l: His Augustness Ohoye-no-izaho-wake, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: rules Empire [after Emperor Nin-Toku] He was one of the august children of Emperor Nin-Toku and Empress Her Augustness Iha-no-hime. He later ruled the Empire.

l: His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake of Tajihi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: rules Empire [after His Augustness Ohoye-no-izaho-wake] He was one of the august children of Emperor Nin-Toku and Empress Her Augustness Iha-no-hime. He later ruled the Empire.

l: His Augustness the Noble Wo-asadzuma-no-waku-go, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: rules Empire [after His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake of Tajihi] He was one of the august children of Emperor Nin-Toku and Empress Her Augustness Iha-no-hime. He later ruled the Empire.

l: Yata-no-waki-iratsume, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: has_tribe Yata Tribe [established as her august proxy] She was wedded by Emperor Nin-Toku, who loved her and sent her a Song. The Yata Tribe was established as her august proxy.

l: Naniha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Naniha is a place associated with imperial rule and dramatic events. Emperor Nin-Toku dwelt there in the palace of Takatsu; its great passage, wave-beaten point, and channel figure in an Empress’s returning voyage and news of his marriage. Later, King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu set Emperor Ri-Chiu’s palace there on fire, which Ri-Chiu saw from the Pass of Hanifu.

l: Empire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Empire is a polity repeatedly ruled by successive emperors and august rulers. It is ruled in turn by Emperor Nin-Toku and later rulers, Emperor Han-Zei, Emperor in-Giyō, His Augustness Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko, Emperor Mu-Retsu, Emperor Kei-Tai, Emperor Kan-an, and Emperor Sen-Kuwa. Its people and officials reject King Karu of Kinashi and support His Augustness Anaho after misconduct. Following Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko’s death, Princes Ohoke and Woke contend over succession, with Woke ruling first. Emperor Mu-Retsu rules eight years; after his death, the Empire is presented to Ohodo, and Emperor Kei-Tai rules from Tamaho at Ihare.

l: august children of Emperor Nin-Toku, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: They numbered six Deities in all, described as five Kings and one Queen. They included His Augustness Ohoye-no-izaho-wake, His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake of Tajihi, and His Augustness the Noble Wo-asadzuma-no-waku-go.

l: Queen Medori, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Queen Medori, Emperor Nin-Toku’s younger half-sister, refused service because of the Empress’s violence, married King Hayabusa-wake, fled with him after her feelings were discovered, and was pursued to Mount Kurahashi and slain by the Imperial army.

l: Empress Iha-no-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Empress Iha-no-hime, exceedingly jealous of the Heavenly Sovereign’s concubines, learns he weds Yata-no-waki-iratsume, discards aralia-leaves, and withdraws to Yamashiro.

l: King Oho-kusaka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Oho-kusaka, brother of Queen Waka-kusaka, agreed to offer her to Prince Oho-hatsuse, sent a ceremonial gift, was slandered, and slain by Emperor an-Kō.

l: remission of taxes and forced labour, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Nin-Toku remitted all people’s taxes and forced labour for three years amid poverty, causing his palace to deteriorate; after prosperity returned, he exacted them again without peasant suffering.

l: Princess Kuro, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Princess Kuro, a regularly beautiful daughter of the Suzerain of Ama in Kibi, served Emperor Nin-Toku, fled toward Kibi fearing the Empress’s jealousy, then hosted the pursuing Emperor there and sang to him.
